idiom_name: Task Parallel Library: Parallel.Invoke / Task.WhenAll on the shared thread pool
implementation_notes: The .NET answer is the TPL: Parallel.Invoke runs an array of actions as one fork/join batch (it returns when all have completed), Parallel.For/ForEach cover data-parallel loops, and Task<T> plus Task.WhenAll expresses dynamic recursive splits - the TPL handles partitioning and schedules the tasks on the shared ThreadPool. Recursive tasks created inside other tasks are queued locally and picked up as cores free up, so the pool-and-deque structure is not written by hand. Hand-built threads and join counters are only justified on runtimes without the TPL or when a custom TaskScheduler must control placement.
pitfalls: Blocking on .Result/.Wait() from a pool thread (sync-over-async) holds a worker and can starve the pool; keep continuations async instead.
Task.WhenAll aggregates exceptions in an AggregateException and Parallel.Invoke throws the first one while letting running actions finish - decide the failure policy at the join.
Parallel.Invoke/For lay out work over the shared ThreadPool; do not nest them inside another parallel region without controlling concurrency (ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism).
